keyVerseText: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
rootMeaning: The name Ἀβραάμ (Abraám) is of Hebrew origin, derived from אַבְרָהָם (ʼAbrâhâm), which means "father of a multitude" or "chief of multitude." This root sense highlights Abraham's role not merely as an individual but as the progenitor of a great nation, emphasizing his foundational position in the history of God's covenant people. The literal meaning enriches the common English usage by connecting Abraham's identity to God's promise of numerous descendants and blessing.
usageInScripture: The term Ἀβραάμ appears 73 times in the New Testament, predominantly translated simply as "Abraham" (41 occurrences), but also in relational forms such as "of Abraham" (18 occurrences) and "to Abraham" (6 occurrences). This range of translations shows the word's consistent use to identify Abraham both as a personal figure and as a patriarchal reference point for lineage and covenantal relationship, underscoring his central role in biblical genealogy and theology.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Abraham as "father of a multitude" is crucial for grasping the biblical narrative of God's covenant faithfulness and election. Abraham embodies the promise that God would establish a people through whom blessing and salvation would come to all nations. His identity as a friend of God and founder of the Hebrew nation points to the divine initiative in salvation history, which ultimately finds fulfillment in Christ. Recognizing Abraham's role helps believers see the continuity of God's redemptive plan and their inclusion in the spiritual descendants of faith.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 1:1 introduces the genealogy of Jesus Christ by identifying Him as "the son of David, the son of Abraham," linking Jesus directly to Abraham. The use of Ἀβραάμ here emphasizes Jesus' fulfillment of the promises made to Abraham, affirming that Christ is the ultimate heir of the covenant and the source of blessing for all nations. This connection roots the gospel in the historic faithfulness of God to His promises and highlights Jesus as the culmination of Abraham's legacy.
